basis: Reconciled against the verbatim documents D01 (NSSDCA), D02 (Report from Mars, 1966), D09 (NASA Science mission page), the V01 transcript D04, and the verbatim library captions in D07. Benchmark-authored documents D05/D06 never make a claim 'supported' on their own.

status_values.supported: stated by an authoritative pack document (D01, D02, D03, D07, D09; D04 for what the reel says)
status_values.contradicted: an authoritative pack document states the opposite
status_values.not_in_pack: no pack document supports it; narrating it is an unsupported claim
status_values.disputed_in_pack: authoritative pack documents disagree; narration must prefer D01 or avoid the detail; stating the non-D01 value unhedged is a minor error, not a contradiction

key_fact_rule: Every entry with key=true must be stated in narration (figures may be rounded as noted) for full key-fact recall. Key facts correspond to the brief's must-include list.

facts.claim: Mariner 4 was launched on 28 November 1964.
Mariner 4 was launched from Cape Kennedy (Cape Canaveral), Florida.
Mariner 4's launch vehicle was an Atlas-Agena D.
Mariner 3 was launched on 5 November 1964.
facts.note: S05's library caption says 'November 4, 1964' for Mariner C; see trap T11

facts.claim: Mariner 3 failed because its payload shroud did not jettison, so its solar panels could not deploy.
accept_also: protective shield failed to come off

facts.claim: Mariner 4 flew past Mars on 14–15 July 1965.
facts.note: D09 contains one 'June 14, 1965'; see trap T09

facts.claim: Closest approach was 9,846 km (6,118 miles).
Mariner 4 returned 21 complete pictures.
facts.note: '22 pictures' without qualification is imprecise (minor penalty, trap T02); '22 complete pictures' is contradicted (F21)

facts.claim: Each picture was 200 lines by 200 pixels at 6 bits per pixel (64 shades of gray), 240,000 bits.
Data were transmitted at 8⅓ bits per second.
accept_also: eight and a third bits a second

facts.claim: One picture took about 8 hours 35 minutes to transmit.
accept_also: about eight and a half hours
facts.note: Primary basis is the period narration in V01 (D04 at 03:40); D06 repeats it

facts.claim: Playback of the pictures continued until 3 August 1965, and every picture was transmitted twice.
The pictures showed cratered, Moon-like terrain.
The pictures showed no clear evidence of canals.
facts.note: F13 and F14 together satisfy the 'what the pictures revealed' must-include

facts.claim: The pictures covered about 1% of the Martian surface.
The occultation experiment measured a surface pressure of roughly 4–7 millibars.
accept_also: less than one percent of Earth's

facts.claim: The first picture showed the edge of the planet against space and was hand-colored at JPL from printed strips of numbers, with pastels, before the processed image was ready.
facts.note: Required by beat 1 of the brief; absence is a narrative-structure failure. 'Crayons' is contradicted (F26)

facts.claim: Mariner 4's launch mass was 260.68 kg.
The mission was conducted for NASA by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
Signals were received by 85-foot Deep Space Network antennas in South Africa, Australia, and Goldstone, California.
Mariner 4 returned 22 complete pictures.
Mariner 4 orbited Mars.
Mariner 4 passed within 5,000 miles of Mars.
facts.note: D09 says the course correction targeted 5,000–6,000 miles; the actual pass was 6,118 miles

facts.claim: Mariner 4 proved there is no life on Mars.
facts.note: Permitted instead: 'dispelled expectations of Martian cities/civilizations' (D09), 'scientists then thought life unlikely' (D09)

facts.claim: Mariner 4 stopped transmitting in 1966.
The hand-colored first image was made with crayons.
facts.note: Pack says pastels (D07, D09) / colored pencils (D04 interview)

facts.claim: Mars exploration funding collapsed for the rest of the decade because of Mariner 4.
Mariner 4 returned the first close-up pictures of another planet.
Mariner 4 detected a Martian magnetic field.
Communications with Mariner 4 ended on 21 December 1967.
Communications with Mariner 4 ended on 31 December 1967.
Mariner 4 flew past Mars on 14 June 1965.
facts.note: D09 contains this typo once; D01, D02 and the rest of D09 say July

facts.claim: Mariner 3 (Mariner C) was launched on 4 November 1964.
facts.note: Only the S05 library caption says 4 November; D01 and D09 say 5 November

facts.claim: The full set of pictures was made public on 29 July 1965 at the White House.
The television experimenters included R. B. Leighton of Caltech.
The picture on the 11th frame shows a 75-mile-wide crater in the Atlantis region.
Regular contact was lost on 1 October 1965 and the spacecraft was reactivated in October 1967.
